findings.issue: One-sided by omission. The prose tells only the patriarchate's coercion of the Catholic party (Ottoman measures, the Gomidas case). The same Ormanian page it cites (4471-4482) goes on: 'The Catholics, in their turn, took advantage of the influence of the French ambassadors to coerce the patriarchate', with the patriarch Avedik of Tokat jailed at the Seven Towers in 1703 through the ambassador's interference and taken to France. Both Catholic sources confirm it: Chamich 21302-21319 (Avedik fined a man of the French ambassador's suite; the ambassador and thirty leading Armenians complained; the vizier had him bastinadoed, stripped of his robes and sent to Tenedos; he died at Marseilles) and Issaverdens 10000-10013 (seized by the French, taken to Marseilles and Paris). Avedik was the patriarch in this movement's own seat, and Ormanian calls the measures on both sides 'weapons of war'. Leaving the reverse pressure out casts the Apostolic church as the only coercer, which misleads in this movement's own voice. Smaller point in the same field: 'In 1664 ... to restore order' follows the Catholic seizure directly, but Ormanian 4383-4388 gives a second cause, Yeghiazar of Aintab proclaiming himself supreme patriarch of Turkey against Etchmiadzin.
findings.fix: longDescription, whole field (FRE 61.0, FK 7.8): "Two seats led the Armenian Apostolic Church in these years. The catholicos lived at Etchmiadzin, in lands ruled from Persia. The Persian court had to approve his election. A patriarch led the Armenians of Constantinople, and that city became the center of the nation. Catholic missionaries worked hard to win Armenians to Rome. One of their party once seized the patriarch's seat, but the people drove him out. A rival bishop also claimed to lead the Armenians of the sultan's lands. In 1664 the catholicos Hacob IV went to Constantinople to restore order. He died there on a second journey in 1680. The quarrel grew bitter. The patriarch's side had the Ottoman government act against Armenians who had become Catholics. The Catholic side, for its part, used the French ambassador against the patriarch. In 1703 the patriarch Avedik was jailed through the ambassador's meddling. He died in France. Catholic writers record that in 1707 the patriarch John handed the priest Gomidas to the Turks, accusing him of following the Franks. \"I am a Christian and a follower of St. Gregory the Illuminator, Armenian by birth,\" Gomidas told them. He was beheaded. In 1742 the pope approved a separate Armenian Catholic patriarchate. Even so, a Catholic Armenian wrote in 1783 that his people still had to obey the patriarch. They still went to his churches to baptize, marry and bury. In 1722 Afghan armies reached Isfahan, and the Armenians of New Julfa had to ransom their town more than once. In 1736 the catholicos Abraham of Crete went to Nadir's camp on the Mughan plain, where an assembly asked Nadir to rule Persia. Abraham was one of three men chosen to speak for the Armenians, and he came home with seven written orders he had asked for. From 1763 to 1780 the catholicos Simeon of Erevan founded a college, brought in printing and built a paper mill. He also opened the church's first ties with the Russian empire. As Persian rule grew harsher, Armenians began to look to the czar. In 1810 a new catholicos, Ephraim, came to Etchmiadzin under a guard of Russian soldiers."  |  relationsSummary, whole field (FRE 61.4, FK 7.8): "The head of the church, the catholicos, sat at Etchmiadzin under Persian rule. A patriarch in the sultan's capital led the Armenians of the Ottoman lands. By the sultan's law, even those who joined Rome had to obey him. Catholic missions won over a party of Armenians, and the patriarch fought back hard. The Catholic party used the French ambassador against him in turn. In 1742 the pope approved a patriarch of their own for the Armenian Catholics. Late in the century, Armenian leaders began to look to Russia." (also fixes A1-08). Add fact-table rows: Ormanian 4473-4475 ('The Catholics, in their turn, took advantage of the influence of the French ambassadors to coerce the patriarchate.'), Ormanian 4475-4478 ('The fate of the patriarch Avedik of Tokat is well known ; through the interference of the king's ambassador, he was first imprisoned at Seven-Towers (1703),'), Chamich 21328-21329 / Issaverdens for death in France, Ormanian 4383-4388 for Yeghiazar. Two-way: this needs the new link in A1-05.

findings.issue: 'Malachia Ormanian ... calls this a defection' makes 'this' the 1742 papal approval. In Ormanian 4469-4472 'This defection' is the bishops Melcon Tasbasian and Abraham Ardzivian openly declaring for Rome at Mardin and Aleppo, before the 1740 see. Wrong referent for a quoted judgment. Also 'the new man' has no antecedent (Issaverdens 10805-10813 is about Abraham's election), and 'Turkish lands' should be 'Ottoman lands' (Serpos: 'Impero Ottomano'). Type, grade (Widely Accepted: Serpos primary for the in-window terms, Ormanian and Issaverdens secondary) and alphabetical id are right; the pair is separately evidenced from the --2 link (1742 hierarchy and the Sis assembly vs. the patriarchate's pressure).
findings.fix: Note (FRE 61.7, FK 7.8): "Two Armenian bishops, one of them Abraham Ardzivian, went over to Rome. Malachia Ormanian, a later Armenian patriarch, calls this a defection. In 1742 the pope approved a new Catholic see with Abraham at its head. A Catholic history says the bishops of Sis met and said his election did not count. Yet in Ottoman lands these Catholics still had no churches of their own." Add Ormanian 4469-4471 to the 'defection' source or extend its lines to 4469-4472 (quote unchanged), and Ormanian 4526-4528 ('The first incumbent was the bishop Abraham Ardzivian (1740),') if the note names him.

findings.issue: Major call: I agree with major:true, but on firmer evidence than the drafter used. Ormanian 4450-4453 names government measures without a law. Serpos 384-387, on this link (its quote is 386-387), names the act itself: 'per le sanzioni Sovrane sono forzati ad ubbidir ... al Patriarca ... autorizzato perciò anche ad infligger pene gravissime contra i renitenti', so sovereign decrees put Armenian Catholics under the patriarch with power to punish (see also Serpos 579-583, 'Leggi rigorose della sublime Porta'). That is a law bearing on a whole group, so outcome_kind 'council-law' fits; 'rule-changed' would also defend. Wording: 'the Turkish state' (note and outcome) is not the sources' term for the period. Ormanian says 'the government', Serpos says 'Impero Ottomano', and the movement's own longDescription says 'Ottoman government'. The note's 'the patriarch was free to punish' drops where that power came from: the sultan's decrees ('autorizzato perciò'). The Issaverdens Gomidas source supports no sentence in the note (harmless, but one sentence could use it).
findings.fix: Note (FRE 62.1, FK 8.0): "The patriarch's side in the capital moved against Armenians who had joined Rome. Those decrees let him punish hard all who would not." Outcome (25 words, FRE 68.9, FK 6.7): "By the sultan's decrees, Armenians who joined Rome still had to obey the patriarch in the capital. He could punish them hard if they refused." outcome_kind: council-law. outcome_evidence: {file: cic/texts/serpos_dissertazione-due-dubbi-armeni-cattolici-ita_1783.txt, lines: '384-387', text: "che 'per le sanzio- ni Sovrane sono forzati ad ubbidir somtriessamente al Patriarca :ddla Nazione residente in Costantinopoli, autorizzato perciò ànchè' ad in- fligger, pene ^vissime contra i- renitenti ;"} (verified verbatim). Extend the Serpos source's lines to 384-387 with this quote.

findings.issue: The note opens with 'Armenian church leaders also fought Rome's claims'. 'also' does not stand alone, and 'Rome's claims' reads more into the sources than they say. Its evidence for Alexander is only the hostile Jesuit line 'guerre secrete aux Catholiques'. A stronger by-name text is vendored: Chamich 21372-21376 says that before his election Alexander 'had written a book expressly to prove the nullity of his power, and the absurdity of being bound by the council of Chalcedon'. For honesty, Chamich 21366-21369 (and Issaverdens 10049-10053) also says that once elected he wrote to the pope in the nation's name. Type, grade and major:false are right.
findings.fix: Note (FRE 75.4, FK 6.7): "Alexander of Julfa wrote a book against the pope's power before he became head of the church. Once elected, he wrote to the pope in the nation's name. Yet a Jesuit report of the time says he waged a secret war on the Catholics. Later Simeon of Erevan, who held the same seat, wrote a book that poked fun at what Rome taught." findings.issue: 'In 1742 the pope gave the Armenian Catholics a patriarch of their own' makes the pope the founder. Ormanian 4523-4536 says Armenians in Cilicia set up the see with two bishops (Abraham Ardzivian, 1740), and the pope sanctioned it in 1742. The longDescription's 'approved' is right.
findings.fix: Covered by the relationsSummary text in A1-01 ('In 1742 the pope approved a patriarch of their own for the Armenian Catholics.').

findings.issue: 'under the same leaders' goes too far. The sources show the same catholicos, Ephraim (Avdall 24081, 24694-24700). The Constantinople patriarch changed (Ormanian 4653-4655: Hovhannes, 1802-1813). The rest is supported: Ephraim backed the Russian Bible Society's plan (24696-24700 'most readily consented'), and the 1810 and 1816 commissions (Ormanian 4671-4680). Type and grade are right.
findings.fix: Note (FRE 66.2, FK 7.8): "The same church carried on past 1815 under the same head. Ephraim, who took his seat at Etchmiadzin in 1810, still led it in 1817, when he backed a Russian society's plan to print the Armenian Bible. In Constantinople, talks with the Catholic party begun in 1810 started again in 1816."

findings.issue: 'councils in the capital would write the church a constitution' does not match Ormanian 4780-4797. Elected councils came first (1841, 1847, 1853). The constitution, 'or Armenian statute', was then worked out (1860) to fix those councils' spheres. The councils did not write it, and it was the nation's statute, not only the church's.
findings.fix: legacy, whole field (FRE 61.9, FK 8.0): "Much of what this church built in these years lasted. Simeon of Erevan's new church calendar met protest at first. Within a short time, every Armenian church used it. Pupils of the patriarch Zakaria founded the college at Armash, which gave the church many later patriarchs and bishops. In the next century, elected councils in the capital would share in running the church, under a written constitution."

checked.facts_confirmed: Each catholicos at Etchmiadzin was elected by the bishops there with the Persian court's approval (Jesuit memoir, c. 1715-25). Constantinople became the center of the nation (Ormanian). Thomas of Aleppo was driven out. Hacob went to Constantinople in 1664 and died there in 1680 (Ormanian; Zakaria gives 2 Aug 1680). Gomidas's story is from Catholic sources, attributed as such: Issaverdens and Chamich, with the quote verbatim and the 1707 beheading. The papal sanction came in 1742. Serpos (1783) shows obedience to the patriarch and use of his churches for baptism, marriage and burial. The Afghans reached Isfahan and Julfa paid ransom (the 1722 date is the margin date, as flagged). At Mughan in 1736 the assembly asked Nadir to rule, Abraham was one of three Armenian speakers, and he got seven raqams (Abraham's own text). Simeon founded a college, a press and a paper mill and opened the first ties with Russia. Ephraim came in 1810 under a Russian guard. The calendar met opposition and then spread to all churches. Armash was founded by Zakaria's pupils. Every voice and its dates are supported (Abraham: 24 Nov 1734 to 17 Apr 1737).
checked.catholic_side_claims: No Catholic-side claim is stated as neutral fact. Gomidas is attributed ('Catholic writers record'), and so is the Jesuit 'one nature' charge. Rightly left out: the Jesuit memoir's claim that Philippos, Hacob IV ('Jacob III') and Yeghiazar were 'fervent Catholics' (3340-3352), and Chamich's story of Nadir's sword. The imbalance runs the other way: the coercion is shown on one side only (A1-01).
checked.turkish_wording: 'the Turks' (Gomidas) follows Issaverdens, and 'Turkey' in modernCountries is fine. 'the Turkish state' and 'Turkish lands' in link text should be 'Ottoman' (A1-02, A1-06). Sources and period both point that way, and the movement's own prose already says 'Ottoman government'.
